utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. May we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, counsel. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. My name is Mark Harmon, appearing with me is Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, Milos Androvic, Eric Tully, Tina Drolec, Novak Lukic, and I'm Gregor Guy-Smith on behalf of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Just before we proceed just to place on the record that the Chamber is sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis this afternoon as Judge David is unavailable. He is held up in the Lukic and Lukic matter. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We would call Richard Butler, Your Honour, as our next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Will you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you so much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Butler. Could you state your full name and spell your last name for the record?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My name is Richard Butler, last name B-u-t-l-e-r.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, did you provide me with a revised curriculum vitae while you were here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have displayed on the monitor, Your Honours, document identification 0649-8346, please. Mr. Butler on the monitor in front of you is a document that at the top of which it says curriculum vitae 1 February, 2009, and has your name on it. Is this a copy of the revised curriculum vitae that you provided me with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could that be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's given a number, and may it please be -- that's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2386.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, this is an extensive curriculum vitae. It's six pages long. I would rather summarize your qualifications, which are set out in this curriculum vitae. I'm going to identify a number of facts from it, and I'm going to ask you merely to affirm if what I have said is accurate. So, first of all, Mr. Butler, your current occupation is a criminal research specialist at the United States Department of Homeland Security Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and you have been holding that position since 2004. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You are a professional -- you have been a professional intelligence officer for 27 years, having served in a variety of military intelligence and civilian law enforcement intelligence positions. You have received intelligence training at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Centre and at the US Army Intelligence Centre and school. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In respect of the events that occurred in Srebrenica, you have prepared a number of reports at the request of the Office of the Prosecutor. You also provided expert testimony about the events in Srebrenica in the Krstic case, the Blagojevic and Djokic case, the Popovic et al case, and in the Krstic appeal before this Tribunal. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In addition, Mr. Butler, you have been qualified as an expert witness beside this court in US federal district court and US immigration courts and in the Special War Crimes Chamber of the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes sir, it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have prepared hard copies of Mr. Butler's expert reports, and I would ask that -- Mr. Butler be provided with copies of those reports so he can refer to them during the course of his evidence, with the Court's consent, and I have discussed it with the Defence, and they have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you confirm, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I'm going to identify the six reports that are going to be -- that have been admitted into evidence pursuant to a Trial Chamber decision of 4 March 2009. Reports that you prepared, and I will identify them, first of all, by exhibit number and then by title of the report. There's P2244; which is the VRS corps command responsibility report; Prosecution Exhibit 2245, which is the Srebrenica military narrative Operation Krivaja; 2246, which is Srebrenica military narrative revised, Operation Krivaja 95; 2247, chapter 8 analytical addendum to the Srebrenica military narrative revised; P2248, VRS brigade command responsibility report; and P2249, VRS Main Staff command responsibility report.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, did you prepare each of those reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I would like to focus on what I will call the narrative reports which are P2245, P2246, and P2247. First of all, Mr. Butler, in respect of P2245 and P2246, did you direct my attention to an error that was in each of those reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could, first of all, have on the screen, P2245, and if we could turn to page 21 of the English, and page 23 of the B/C/S. Well, I -- I'm not sure in 2245 if that is the ... it's page 21 of the English in P2245.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm informed that's page 28 of e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm just --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's paragraph 4.6 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excellent, thank you. Just briefly, since you mentioned it, he directed your attention to an error, I have not received any proofing notes. Are there any?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I sent an e-mail to you yesterday, identifying the -- Ms. Javier did, identifying the error, and there are no proofing notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, very well. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, I would like to direct your attention, if I could, to paragraph 4.6 in this report. Can you identify the error and tell us what correction you would like to make in paragraph 4.6.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In paragraph 4.6, the second to the last sentence referring to the presidents of the civilian commissioner for Srebrenica Mr. Miroslav Deronjic and Ljubisav Simic needs to be struck, as well as footnote citation 105. That is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Butler, if we turn to the Prosecution Exhibit 2246, again, referring to paragraph 4.6. And I will give you the e-court page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Pages 40 and 41, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, paragraph 4.6, it goes over to the next page as well, but do you see an error in paragraph 4.6, and would you like to correct it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again, the second to the last sentence in the paragraph discussing the presence of Mr. Deronjic and Mr. Simic, that sentence needs to be struck, as well as footnote citation 215.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the identical error appeared in both reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. With that correction completed, Mr. Butler, I'd like to turn to Prosecution Exhibit 2245 again. And in the introduction to that report, you identified the tasks, the primary objectives, that you had been given in respect of preparing this particular report. Could you just refer to the introduction of this report and in the -- identify, if you would do so, Mr. Butler, what your primary objectives were in respect of the preparation of this report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, as noted in the second and third paragraph in the introduction, my objectives in this particular report were related to proceedings of the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Krstic. In that respect, my first mission was to detail the linkage with respect to the Drina Corps commander, his staff, his subordinate units with the criminal acts as charged in the indictment. The second objective dealt with the issue of the specific role and responsibilities of General Krstic within the framework of the army of the Republika Srpska. First as the Chief of Staff and Deputy Commander of the Drina Corps, and later as the commander of the Drina Corps during the period of the crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, you prepared a revised narrative, which is P2246, about two years later. Can you tell us what the objectives were in respect of P2246.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Those are laid out in the third and fourth paragraph. This revised narrative was in response to the trials of Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic, both of whom were individuals at the brigade level, rather than corps level for the same crime base. So my goal was to then to examine in detail the issue of their particular roles and responsibilities within the army of the Republika Srpska during the period within the context of a brigade, as well as to determine what linkage there was with respect to documents and other materials dealing with the involvement of those particular brigades with the crime scenes as charged. The third component of this was also to continue to deal with the issue of the ongoing appeal of General Krstic, and in that respect to update information that had come in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor relating to issues that were active under appeal, particularly with respect to the point in time that he assumed command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, in your introduction in Prosecution Exhibit 2246 on page 1V, middle of the page, you identify the methodology that you used as primarily a document based analytical approach. Was this methodology used in both reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you explain what you mean when you say a document based analytical approach?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In describing it, it represents the fact that the material available that I used for my military analysis for the most part consisted of documents and other like information that was in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor. Those included military records from the various military units of the Drina Corps. We call documents, but it -- somewhat separate is the intercepts of Bosnian Serb army communications that were in transcript form that we had possession of. It included material derived from open source media. Could be newspapers, it could be videos, could be other types of information like that. What it does not include as a general rule is witness statements or witness testimony, because I was cognizant obviously at the time that it is the role of the Trial Chamber to ultimately hear that type of testimony from the witnesses involved. So where I do incorporate witness testimony into these narrative reports, it is only for the purpose of setting the context of the act as it occurred. It is not for individuals to rely on as either a definitive version of what happened or why. It just sets the context so that when I explain and lay out where the documents and where intercepts and where other pieces of information fit in context to that, the reader has the -- the ability to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now when you say open source, did that include military magazines? Magazines from the VRS, for example?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I request that Mr. Harmon does not lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm trying to get through this element fairly quickly. I will withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you expand on what you mean by open source materials, Mr. Butler? Be more detailed and more precise.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It would include print media from western sources. It would include print media from Bosnia, print media from Serbia and the Republika Srpska. It did include military magazines. It included civilian magazines. It included video that was both broadcast on air as well as private video that was taken from a number of sources. It would include that broader genre of information that's normally associated with media reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, what selection criteria did you use when you were going through this -- this group of documents that you considered?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The selection criteria was only limited on the basis of the actual conduct of the crime as charged by the Office of the Prosecutor. It's not my goal in either of these reports to lay out either a definitive history of East Bosnia or even the Srebrenica crime base. So to that respect, the initial goal as reflected by the early versions of the narrative reflect the period of 1 through 30 July 1995 as the period of the initial crimes related to Srebrenica and follow on through August, September, October, because of the involvement of various units of the Drina Corps in the process of concealing the crimes by exhuming and then later reburying the victims of those crime. It does not go into great detail into the events that occurred prior to that, only to set up context, or after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, you arrived at a number of conclusions in your report. And let me, first of all, direct you to the paragraph 1218 which is in Prosecution Exhibit 2245. In this conclusion, Mr. Butler, I'd like you to explain to the Trial Chamber what conclusions you reached in respect of the VRS Main Staff's involvement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Can you repeat the paragraph, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Paragraph 1218 of Prosecution Exhibit 2245.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The conclusion that I reached with respect to the Main Staff was that they were a significant participant in the planning, decisions, and execution of the events that were surrounding the criminal acts as charged. They issued orders. Their officers were on the ground as these orders occurred, in many cases. The orders that they issued to their subordinate formations, the Drina Corps, were acted upon and responded to, either directly by the Drina Corps or by their subordinate formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what conclusions, Mr. Butler, did you reach in respect of whether the Drina Corps members were active in the planning and execution of the crimes committed during the time-frame you were looking at?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The same, sir. The Drina Corps was part of this entire planning and execution process.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if I can direct your attention in that report to paragraph 13.23, is that where you set out your conclusions or a portion of your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And did you come to any conclusions in this context about whether the chain of command in the Drina Corps to the Main Staff was functioning?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And, in fact, my conclusion was that during the period that the chain of command, as organised in the VRS along the former JNA lines was functioning as it was supposed to during the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Butler, did you after reviewing the documentation that was available to you, come to any conclusions in respect of whether the crimes that are described in -- in the Krstic indictment and the Blagojevic indictment dealing with mass executions and dealing with the forcible transfer of the population from Potocari, did you reach any conclusions as to whether those crimes were planned and organised?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did, and it was my conclusion that those crimes were, in fact, planned and organised in a very sophisticated manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, just to enlighten the Trial Chamber, what when you say -- when you refer to your conclusion, "these were planned and organised crimes," can you set forth the elements that led to you believe and what -- led to you believe these were planned and organised crimes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The scope of the crimes involved, as well as the variety of military units and staff officers and functions that were part of them relates to just how wide the involvement of both the planning and the execution was of the Drina Corps. For example, the widespread effort to gather the requisite transportation and the fuel that had to go behind both moving the civilian population out of Potocari, as well as then moving the prisoners who were detained in and around Bratunac to the execution sites. The efforts of the military police as well as military units to escort these prisoners and then to guard them at various locations, schools in the Zvornik brigade area. The efforts of various officers in attempting to find individuals who would be actually engaged in the execution of these individuals and to ensure that they were secured in the schools. The efforts of these same officers to organise the engineering equipment necessary to bury the mass quantities of bodies on the battlefield -- or not at the battlefield but at these execution sites, as well as later on the efforts of these same officers, once the crimes had been discovered by the international community and publicised to go in and re-exhume these bodies and bury them in more remote locations. So from a military perspective, when you have to look at the wide variety of tasks that have to happen for a military organisation to accomplish that, it is a fairly wide scope of the unit. And then, of course, when you have the intercept information, the intercepts confirm that many officers who are key officers on the Drina Corps staff as well as the Main Staff were actively involved in that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in the course of the preparation of the Krstic report, did -- was there an issue and did you consider the issue of when General Krstic assumed command of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there was an issue, and I certainly did consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what conclusion did you reach in respect of when General Krstic became commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: My conclusion was that General Krstic became commander of the Drina Corps in the early evening hours of 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, let's focus on the additional reports that you prepared, three reports. I call them the command responsibilities reports. P2244, which is the VRS corps command responsibility report; P2248, which is the VRS brigade command responsibility report; and P2249, which is the VRS Main Staff command responsibility report. Can you, first of all, identify what your tasks were in respect of these particular reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The preparation of these reports actually predated the preparation of the narrative reports. As the foundational step, my task in these particular cases were to, within the framework of the army of the Republika Srpska, as well as the legal framework within the Republika Srpska at the time, to identify the army, where it fit within the law, to identify the doctrine that the army was using, in this case the former doctrine of -- the doctrine of the former Yugoslav national army, to determine that the VRS was still in fact using that doctrine as their -- the way that they operated in the battlefield, understanding the hierarchy of the army of the Republika Srpska, how it went from the very top echelons down to the lowest echelons, and then what the roles and responsibilities were in practice as well as under law of the individuals in question, whether they be a corps commander, whether they be a corps Chief of Staff, a brigade commander, or any of the other various officers. So for me, that was the foundational step, before I could -- and understanding their roles and responsibilities within their own military forces before I could go to the next step of figuring out what their impact was with respect to the Srebrenica operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, what methodology did you use in preparing these reports, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Again, primarily because it was all we had at the time, it was a documents-based approach, based on various military documents that we had, based on translations of the former Yugoslav national army doctrinal regulations for corps and brigades. The same with their former manuals for the functioning of the security service and the military police, their command and staff manuals which explains how their staff processes worked and how their officers were trained. And then later on, although not incorporated in my report, when we had access to a number of those high ranking officers, the ability to go out, explain what my conclusions were and to determine whether or not, you know, my thesis on how it worked was in fact the way that they operated. And they were able to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, could you briefly describe --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I might interject. I'd appreciate if the witness confines his answers to the questions asked and not go astray from those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can you briefly describe the conclusions you reached on the basis of the work that you performed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The conclusions that I reached on the basis of those command responsibility reports was that in almost all respects the army of the Republika Srpska operated in the same manner that the officers were trained under the former JNA. They used the same operating guidance and same methodologies, and that their units, be them of corps or brigade or lower levels, were in large part organised in accordance with the way that the JNA manuals had described.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in your report P2245, just to orient --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to take you back to the point you made a little earlier on. On what basis did you come to the conclusion that Radoslav Krstic became commander of the Drina Corps some time in the early evening of the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sir, in that particular context when you look at the initial version of the narrative and the corps command report, our basis of knowledge from the orders that are signed by him reflect the fact that he is signing orders as the corps commander sometime -- at, I believe, 2000 hours on 13 July 1995. General Krstic, of course, his position was that even though it said that he wasn't the commander, he was in fact some other form of commander. As the years went on investigative ly, the OTP was able to obtain additional documents that in fact show the formal change over of command, and also I understand that there has in fact been witness testimony that reflects that that change of command occurred roughly 1900 hours, 2000 hours on 13 July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what is the date of the formal change of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 13 July, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 13 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I intend to introduce that document in the course of Mr. Butler's evidence, just for your information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may then proceed. I'll stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your report, Mr. Butler, Prosecution Exhibit 2245, and in chapter 2 of that report you identify the units of the Drina Corps and the VRS Main Staff and the key person nationalities associated with each of those units. And at the end of that report, you prepared four organigrams showing the structure of the VRS Main Staff, the Drina Corps, the Zvornik Brigade, and the Bratunac brigade. And you identified -- populated that organigram with the personalities associated with each of those positions. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, based on my knowledge at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now let me -- let's turn, if we can, Mr. Butler, to the attack that took place on the UN Safe Area of Srebrenica. You refer to those in your -- in Prosecution exhibit 2246 in chapter 3 of the report. Mr. Butler, what was Operation Krivaja? What was it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Krivaja was the code-name of a VRS military operation whose initial goal was to reduce the size of the safe haven around Srebrenica to a very small area, almost within the urban environs of the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did that change -- did that plan change?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, based on the unanticipated success that the military units were having, some time on the evening hours of 9 July 1995, the plan changed, and it then became the capture of the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you identify which VRS units participated in the attack on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. A variety of units participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: They would include a tactical group form from the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, Drina Corps; a tactical group from the Birac Infantry Brigade, Drina Corps; tactical group from the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, the Drina Corps asset; it would include troops from the surrounding military unit, the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, it's a Drina Corps asset; elements of the Drina Corps artillery were involved; as well as elements of the Milici Light Infantry Brigade; and the Skelani separate battalion, both also Drina Corps units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What role, if any, did the 10th Sabotage Detachment play in the events?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Once the decision was made to actually go into the urban area of Srebrenica, the 10th Sabotage Unit as well as some other special police units were brought in to perform that function. They were placed under the control of the Drina Corps for that operation, and in fact they were one of the lead units that actually went into the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, what we're going to do and the way we're going to progress through a large part of your evidence today is we're going to be taking a look at film footage from the events surrounding the takeover of Srebrenica and the forcible transfer of persons from that enclave as well as the capture and detention and killings of people who had surrendered to the VRS. Now, you mentioned earlier in your evidence that you had considered film footage from various open sources. In the course of looking at this evidence, we're going to see the source of some of this footage that will be identified --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For counsel's benefit and for Your Honour's benefit, will be identified in the portions of the film that identify what the theme is of the ensuing film. Now, one of those, Your Honours, will say Petrovic footage. And I want to clarify with Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Butler, are you familiar with Petrovic footage? Can you explain to the court who Petrovic was.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am familiar it. It was one of the pieces of material I actually used in my report. Zoran Petrovic was a reporter, an independent reporter from Belgrade. On the day of 13 July 1995, he was permitted to accompany Republika Srpska special police commander Borovcanin in and around the area of Potocari as well as along the road from Bratunac to Kravica, to Sandici, towards the Konjevic Polje. During his period accompanying him on 13 July, he videotaped a good deal of the events that were occurring in those locations on that day. Those videotapes identify locations where individuals were detained. They identify one location where individuals were executed, and they show in some degree of detail the actual separation process that occurred in the town of Potocari on 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, what other sources of video footage that we will be looking at can you identify for the Court?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Other sources would include video footage of -- or that was taken by members of the VRS themselves. There was a video crew there from the VRS Main Staff that was taking video that ultimately ended up on Republika Srpska television, so there's a good deal of video from that. There's also one small piece of video that is from an independent Dutch production crew that obtained that video footage sometime after the war, which shows some scenes related to Potocari and also Sandici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say obtained sometime after the war, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The video footage was in a Dutch documentary that I believe came out, if I recall correctly, sometime in 1999. I know that the investigation team has the full background on the process of how they obtained the video and where. I don't recall the details of that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. It is that detail that I wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, what I intend to do is show a series of videos. I will stop it at various points. I will note the timer number on it because there are some portions that I'd ask Mr. Butler to identify. If we could take a look at the first clip. It 65 ter 4459I -- 4559I.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have stopped -- we have stopped this at 53.-- 00.00.53.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, even though this is the backside of this individual's head, can you identify who this individual is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is Colonel Vinko Pandurevic, the commander of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And for reference, Your Honour, the paragraph he's referred to in chapter 2, and he is -- identified in paragraph 3.2 and other parts of the narrative. If we could continue, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we be told where this place is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can you identify -- you have seen this footage before. Can you identify where this is taking place, Where this footage is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is on the road from Zeleni Jadar moving towards Srebrenica. It's actually a downhill grade, so the main axis of attack went down this particular road, down the valley towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what day is this, approximately? Do you have any idea of dating this particular film footage, or a range of dates when this was taken?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: This film footage, I believe, all comes from the day that Srebrenica was captured. This would be the morning/early afternoon hours of 11 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could -- if that is satisfactory, Your Honour, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We've stopped the film at 00.01.38.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can you identify this individual, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is Captain Milan Jolovic. He is the commander of the Drina Wolves unit of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what was the Drina Wolves units?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The Drina Wolves were a rather elite combat formation. They were considered the assault battalion of the Drina Corps, although they were normally subordinate to the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. This particular unit made up some of the best-trained and fittest soldiers of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, first of all, before we ask you some more questions on that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could that be given an exhibit number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2387.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, at the time this film footage was occurring, were there members of the Bosnian army in the enclave, the -- the Bosnia -- army of the government of Bosnia, ABiH is what I refer to it commonly and what is referred in your report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In fact, despite the UN presence, the enclave was never disarmed, and the military formation of the ABiH 2 Corps was the 28th Infantry Division that had a sizeable presence inside Srebrenica and the surrounding enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And can you describe the arms that was available to them.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Mostly what we would consider light arms, individual weapons, pistols, rifles, machine-guns, small crew-served weapons, heavier machine-guns and mortars. Given the fact that they could not supply themselves under normal circumstances, that they had to smuggle weapons and ammunition in, either through known smuggling corridors or, you know surreptitious helicopter flights, or by other means, they couldn't have and didn't have any particularly heavy weapons. But they did have a considerable number of light arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did they have heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: There were some heavy weapons that existed prior to the establishment of the safe area, but those particular weapons were in the UN weapons storage area and under UN control. They were not part of this July 1995 fight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You referred to surreptitious helicopter flights. How surreptitious were these, and how often were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They're -- from the readings of the VRS documents, they were aware that on at least a biweekly basis that Bosnian Muslim military forces would fly helicopters to the enclaves to drop off ammunition to pick up individuals or to deliver high-ranking or high-value individuals, occasionally take out a seriously wounded individual. They were aware they were doing that, and took active measures in order to try and prevent that. I think in one particular case in either January/February 1995, they were successful in shooting down one of those helicopters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And did they see the contents of the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the answer it that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know how they came to the conclusion of -- the conclusion about the mission of these helicopters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How the Bosnian Serbs did?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. You say from the documents of VRS, this is how you came it that conclusion. From the reading of those documents, how did they come to the conclusion about the mission of those helicopters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sir, they -- they, like everyone else, they had intelligence means that were involved. They had sources of information inside the enclave. It -- while it was done clandestinely, it was common knowledge within military circles that this was happening. So they were aware that these helicopters were coming in. And in fact in some cases their ability to track them was highlighted by the fact that they would get radar information from the VJ and through their own air defence early warning network so that these were coming at various points in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can understand being aware of the helicopter coming. I'm sure, even by the naked eye, if are you in the vicinity you might be able to see. What I'm trying to find out is how the mission of the helicopter and the contents of the helicopter were determined.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, sir, it was -- I can only tell you what the documents say, that it was common knowledge to them. I believe that in the course of the Office of the Prosecutor's investigation into this, they have also been able to confirm what those flights were about. So I don't -- you know, the fact that I can't tell you exactly how they knew of this, but can I tell that, you know, as time went by, they were correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just asked these questions because we have just heard testimony about this part of the case, which goes against what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You understand. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to ask a question. We heard another witness who told us that it was impossible that helicopter flew into Srebrenica. They could not go into the enclaves in Srebrenica without the UNPROFOR people realizing it. This witness worked for the United Nations and told us he was the spokesperson, and he said that he did not see any report to that effect mentioning, for instance, a helicopter or a flight of a helicopter arriving into one of the enclaves. How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I certainly can't vouch for that individual. I can tell that you they happened. Certainly with respect to the Srebrenica enclave, it was a well-known fact that the Bosnian Muslim forces, the 28th Infantry Division --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I would like to you be very clear. You can tell us it happened, or you can tell us that you read VRS documents stating that it happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I can tell you it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It happened. You saw it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not being an eye-witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm not trying to do that. But what I'm saying is that approximately a month and a half before Srebrenica that the entire Command Staff, for the most part, of the 28th Division left the Srebrenica enclave and ended up in Tuzla where they were part of -- where they were 2 corps undergoing training and some other types of issues. They flew out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I must ask you this question. About a month before the taking of Srebrenica, you were in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. Again what I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you see, I'm concerned about the way you are testifying. You're testifying like an eye-witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, and I don't mean to, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, don't then. If are you not an eye-witness, don't testify like that. If you have heard or if you've read about it somewhere, say this is what you read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, sir, I can tell you that the VRS understood that these helicopter flights were occurring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't want to know at this stage what the VRS understood. I want to know what you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you testifying to something that you saw? Are you testifying to something that you read about? Are you testifying to something that you were told?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm testifying to the information that I read about in the VRS reports, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can only say the VRS reports state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But the other portion of that is that it an attempt to -- in analysing this, to verify these, the investigation did look at these issues, and our understanding from the ongoing investigation is that the VRS information in this regard was accurate and that these flights were taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it possible, then, Witness, and this is my question: Is it possible that the UN observers, the UN military observers, hadn't seen anything? It is not such a huge space, Srebrenica. How is it possible that they hadn't heard anything, they hadn't seen the helicopters? How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ma'am, as a component of the Srebrenica investigations and three trials, a large number of Dutch officers who were in the enclave during that period testified, and they made it very clear that their ability to move around the enclave completely and have full freedom of movement was severely restricted by the forces of the 28th Infantry Division. They openly acknowledge that there was a large part of the enclave that they never had access to, because that is where the military formations of the 28th Division operated. It is it entirely possible that United Nations observers, and in fact as the Dutch report, in their own reporting, there are large parts of the enclave that they were not able to observe and were not able to know what type of activity was happening there, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Even with the help of radars, they could not detect anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ma'am, the Dutch did not have any air defence early warning radars in and around the Srebrenica area, as far as I'm aware. While I'm sure NATO had radar coverage of that area, I have no way of knowing how much information was shared by the NATO deny-flight missions with the United Nations on that basis. I -- frankly, I guess I apologised in so much as I didn't believe that that would possibly be a disputed fact. I thought that was pretty much common knowledge that those flights were occurring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. The only point, sir, is that you're called here as an expert witness, and what we ask -- what we expect of you is opinion evidence, not fact evidence, unless you say, These are the facts that I have been given to operate on. But not facts that you claim to have seen or observed somewhere. Because you're not coming in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Agreed, sir, and certainly I do not want to ever leave that impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We happen to have that impression.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, did the members of the 28th Division resist the advance of the VRS into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: No, sir, not particularly heavily. Their strategy was, in part, to have the United Nations defend the enclave, so what would happen is that when they were contacted by the VRS forces, they would withdraw back behind the United Nations, the Dutch troops, and put the Dutch in a position where they would have fire on the Serbs or essentially have their positions overrun.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What actions did the members of the 28th Division take in the face of the VRS invasion into the safe area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: While there was some token resistance. For the most part the forces of the 28th Infantry Division just continued to withdraw towards the town of Srebrenica and to the hills to the west of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice we're a little bit early from the break time, but the next clip I'm going to show is going to carry over. It will be -- it will either take us past the break by a few minutes, or we can break now and we can reconvene, and I can start afresh. I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What are you asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think it is better to break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, in a moment, we're going to look at some film footage from the town of Srebrenica that was taken on 10th of July, 1995. Before we look at that film, can you tell me what the distance, approximate distance is between the town of Srebrenica and the town of Potocari, both of which were located in the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that, by road, it's approximately 4 to 5 kilometres, maybe a little less.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So if we could play 65 ter 4459.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're sure it's 4459?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, I'm not. I've been corrected once again, Your Honour. I have been corrected once again. It's 4559J.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we've stopped the film at 00.06.08.7. Can you identify the type of weapon that is being fired in this particular frame?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, there's no foundation for an expertise with regard to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll refrain -- I'll lay the foundation then, Your Honour. I mean, I think you've --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, how long did you serve in the United States Army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Twenty years, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you participate in weapons training and weapons usage?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: As part of my role as an intelligence warrant officer, I was required to be familiar with the weaponry of less the United States forces but more so of the former Soviet Union Warsaw Pact and adversaries. So a knowledge of those types of weapons is what I'm trained to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, then are you in a position to tell what kind of a weapon is being fired in this particular frame?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is a mortar. I believe from the size, 82-millimetres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And where are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the beginning of the clip, Your Honour, the clip identified the town of Srebrenica, so -- and I identified at the beginning of Mr. Butler' evidence, we were now going to go to look at footage from the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And can I ask, if Your Honour wishes, because we can locate this quite easily in the rest of this film, but if you're satisfied, Your Honour, I will proceed, or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, at the time this weapon is being fired, what -- on the 10th of July, in respect of the town of Srebrenica, can you put this footage in context with the events?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Sir, I believe this footage is actually the 11th of July, approximately the middle morning hours. This is the last rear guard elements of the 28th Division. What happens is -- the next component is this is where all of the civilians, particularly the women and the children, are congregating around the United Nations Dutch Bravo company compound that was actually located in Srebrenica town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Butler, at this point, this clip has been identified as the 10th of July. I want to explore that with you because we are going to be looking at a clip that is dated the 11th of July where we will be looking at the town of Srebrenica and civilians. What is it that makes you conclude that this is the 11th of July, as opposed to what was on the caption of the film, the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Again, sir, it's been a few years since I have seen a lot of this footage. I always see in the same streaming portion associated with the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's continue then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, we've stopped the film at 00.06.41.8. Can you identify the building that says "UN Srebrenica" on it? What is that building?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is the Bravo company compound of the Dutch battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, we've stopped this film at 00.07.32.9, and in the left-hand corner of this footage, one can see the date, 10/7/1995.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could continue then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I'm going to ask you to -- we're going to look at some film footage from the 11th of July, 1995, and to put this footage into context, can you just inform the Court what was happening in the enclave on the 11th of July, based on your review of the documents and other materials available to you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: At this particular time, the Bosnian Serb army forces, the Drina Corps, are located in the heights around the town. The Bosnian Muslim leadership in the enclave has made the decision that they're going to abandon the enclave. And what ends up happening is you have two separate routes out of the enclave, one large group of civilians, primarily women, children, elderly men, elect to accompany the Dutch Bravo company forces out of the town. Another group, the military-aged men, or those believed to be, you know, within the military age group, start assembling at a series of villages, Susnjari, Jaglici, near Potocari, and they begin to make an overland trek from the former enclave area to what they considered to be free territory near Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if we could play this particular footage that's entitled: Srebrenica Town, 11 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we've stopped the film at 00.14.22.6. Can you tell us what this particular portion of the film depicts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This depicts one portion of what we generally refer to as the column of military-aged men that's assembling and beginning to move towards the ABiH 2 Corps lines near Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could 65 ter 4559J be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And just for purposes of my own record keeping, that includes two separate clips, one on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The 10th of July and the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what's the provenance of this film?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have to go back and -- I can check on that. It would say at the -- probably at the beginning of the film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the provenance of that film is Muslim -- it's Muslim civilian footage. It's footage that was taken in the enclave by somebody who was in the enclave at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'd like to know who that somebody is. That's what I mean by provenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll see if I can find that out for you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar, would you please assign an exhibit number to that clip so it can be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2388.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, based on your review of the documents and materials available and with you -- that were available to you, can you just generally describe the column, the direction of travel of the column, and what happened to the column, in general terms?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In general terms, the column formed up at the villages of Susnjari and Jaglici through the evening hours of 11th July and -- or through the evening hours of 10 July to 11 July and began to move almost in single or double file, because of the extensive minefields around the enclave, down known smuggling routes by which the ABiH had actually been bringing in the weapons. The Bosnian Serb military and police forces knew where those routes were and, as a result, they were able to set up ambushes throughout the course of this column, moving from that location, the former enclave, to their destination. Starting the evening of the 12th and running from the 13th, 14th, 15th, 16th, there was a good deal of combat activity that occurred between the armed members of the column, as well as the Republika Srpska police and the Republika Srpska military units that were trying to block that column. One of the unique aspects about that that comes from through from the military and police documents is that the army leadership and, to a lesser degree, the police leadership under estimated the size of the column as well as potential military threat that that column faced towards the Zvornik municipality. So as time goes on and as the times as these leaders recognise the size and the potential threat of this column, one sees a great deal of reallocations of military and police forces from other areas on the battlefield in order to deal with it. Ultimately on the 16th of July, because of the combat that is occurred and because of the situation in the Zvornik brigade, the Zvornik brigade military commander Colonel Pandurevic, makes a decision that allows for a large portion of that column to pass through his lines and ultimately make it to friendly territory. That cease-fire lasted for 24 hours. Afterwards the Zvornik brigade and other forces there moved in to close that off, and then the remainder of the column is systematically tracked down and either captured or killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON

One of the unique aspects of this operation here is that the VRS, as is apparent through the documents and the military intercepts of their communications, they are unaware of a decision by the Muslim forces to try to break out of the former enclave. utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. On the outside or on the perimeter of the enclave itself, the Dutch, the UN, had established observation posts so they could monitor activity to some degree. Those that did, and for the most part most of the of the OPs did, were taken to the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac where they remained.

utterances.text: Okay, if we could continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have stopped at 1.50.24.7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To the right of Mr. Simic, the second person from the right wearing a camouflage uniform, who is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: That's Dragomir Vasic. He is the head of the security centre for Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And to his right in a blue -- it looks like a blue blazer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Miroslav Deronjic. At this time he is the civilian commissioner for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And to his right, the far left of the image, he has a moustache and it looks like a camouflage vest?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: That is Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We've stopped at 1.50.27.1. Are you able to identify the person to the right of Colonel Popovic? Colonel Popovic at this time has a glass to his mouth.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And the person seated at the end of the table on the left, who is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: That person is Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that the language on the bottom will also be part of the record. And I noticed that when Colonel Karremans was talking, he says, Is it suitable for a meeting. And the language is not contained in the actual written part right -- as here. I don't know whether or not that makes a difference or not with regard to the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I -- we'll listen to this again. I accept my colleague's observation. It doesn't make any difference in terms what this film portrays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought that language was written in the centre of the -- of the clip as they interpret.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You may be well -- you may well be right, Your Honour. It's just as I was listening to Colonel Karremans talk, I heard him say, Is it was suitable. And I didn't see that particular language. I was just raising the issue, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you just scroll. Can you rewind a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Maybe I missed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see what you're saying. Yes, it is there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, based on your review of the documents and the materials available to you, do you know what time this meeting ended, and do you know what happened shortly after this meeting, in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The meeting ended at approximately 1130 hours. And shortly thereafter, many of the VRS officers who were at this meeting, as well as, of course, the Dutch, returned to Potocari. And then shortly after that, a number of buses and trucks start showing up in Potocari to begin moving the civilian population out of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know how many Muslim civilians were in Potocari on that day, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Reports tend to vary from what the VRS reports versus what the United Nations reports. I think the total number or generally accepted number is about 35.000 people were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 4559O on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We've stopped at 1.54.41.7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you able to identify which units these soldiers belonged to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. These are individuals who are members of the 2nd Sekovici Special Police Unit, that is a member of the Republika Srpska special police brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And under whose command were they on this date?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: They were directly commanded by the Deputy Commander of the special police brigade, Ljubo Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And under whose command was he operating?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: He was operating under military control, so it would have been General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Can we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask this question to clarify your last answer, Mr. Butler. This film is taken in the morning of the 13th of July. Would those soldiers have been under the command at that particular point in time of General Krstic or General Zivonovic, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. Perhaps I'm mistaken. When we started this film, it indicated that it was the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: 12th of July. I meant the 12th of July. That's correct. Thank you, counsel. 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, would these soldiers have been under the command of General Krstic who I understood was the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir and General Zivonovic remains the corps commander, but shortly after this period, General Zivonovic goes back to his command post in around the Vlasenica area. General Krstic is the senior officer of the Drina Corps who remains on the ground at the time, so they are under his control. So I guess you could call it they are still under General Zivanovic's command, but General Krstic is actually in charge of the particular operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We've stopped the film at 1.55.51.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in the image on the right-hand side you can see two DutchBat soldiers, blue helmets and carrying rifles. Mr. Butler, are you able, based on that image with those soldiers and those weapons they're carrying, to put an approximate time on this particular film clip on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It would be the early afternoon hours, noon, 1300, maybe 1400 at the latest. One of the things that the Dutch report is that as soon as Bosnian Serb military and police forces start entering the compound at Potocari, one of the things that they do is begin to systematically disarm the Dutch soldiers. So by the late afternoon hours on 12 July 1995, the Dutch have effectively been disarmed by the Republika Srpska police and military forces that are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're going to replay -- play this for just a minute. I want to identify one person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay, if you, Mr. Butler, I'd like you -- we've stopped the film at 1.57.29.5. And there's an individual who appears to be throwing something toward the children. He is on the left-hand side of this image; he's wearing a camouflage uniform. Can you identify him?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is Ljubisav Borovcanin. He is the deputy commander of the Republika Srpska special police brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We've stopped the film at 1.59.48.6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, in the upper left-hand corner there's a logo. Are you able to identify that logo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Same symbol as before. That's Serbia Radio and Television.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, this is stopped at 2.03.09.2. The soldier in the middle of this image with his arm, his right arm on his hip, who is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Again, sir, this is it General Major Radislav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Do you know where this film clip was taken?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: This film clip was actually taken at Potocari. As it pans along, you will see one of the buildings there located in Potocari as well as the buses going by.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have stopped the film at 02.04.05.6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And General Krstic is the individual in the middle of this image. To his left in the background there is a figure who is walking in General Krstic's direction. Can you identify that individual, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: That, sir, is Colonel Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Vujadin Popovic, who we have seen in other film clips?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The assistant commander for security for the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now we have a new interview that is taking place. We've stopped the film at 02.04.26.5. And the person being interviewed, the second individual from the left wearing a camouflage uniform, who is he, and what is his position?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: He is Mr. Zoran Kovakovic. He is the company commander of the 4th Infantry Company of the 2nd battalion of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Over his left soldier, appearing directly over his left soldier is a bald man with a black moustache. Who is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric, the chief of intelligence of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And can you tell me where this interview is taking place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Also in Potocari, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this film clip be given an exhibit number and admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The film clip is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2393.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this should be an appropriate time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, unfortunately, we have not been able to finish with you today, so you are going to have to come back tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon in the same courtroom. I believe you have been testifying here several times. You must be knowing the procedure, but it is my duty it repeat it to you. While you are on the witness stand, you may not discuss the case with anybody, not even with Mr. Harmon or anybody from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. The matter stands adjourned until tomorrow, at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, Courtroom II. Court adjourned.
